ncert.chapter_hint: Moving Charges and Magnetism (magnetic force, cyclotron, force on a current)

notes: 11 Objective I items rebuilt. Several source items are a linked family comparing electron/proton/He⁺/Li⁺ on force, radius and frequency; these are kept as a group since the contrast between the three quantities is the teaching point.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Magnetic Field
practice_bank.intro: Eleven questions on magnetic force. The one fact that resolves half of them: a magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it can never change a particle's speed.

sections.title: Force on a Moving Charge
sections.blurb: Perpendicular to both the velocity and the field — always.

items.prompt: A positively charged particle projected towards the east is deflected towards the north by a magnetic field. The field may be directed
items.explanation: With $ \vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B} $, take east as $ \hat{i} $, north as $ \hat{j} $ and up as $ \hat{k} $. We need $ \hat{i} \times \vec{B} $ to point along $ \hat{j} $, and since $ \hat{i} \times (-\hat{k}) = +\hat{j} $, the field must point *downward*. A field along the velocity (east or west) would give no force at all.

items.prompt: A charged particle is whirled in a **horizontal** circle on a frictionless table by a string. A magnetic field is switched on in the **vertical** direction. The tension in the string
items.explanation: The magnetic force is $ qvB $ directed radially — inward or outward depending on the signs of the charge and the field and the sense of rotation. If it points inward it helps the string and the tension falls; if outward, the string must pull harder. Without knowing those signs, either is possible.

items.prompt: Of an electron, a proton, a $ \text{He}^{+} $ ion and a $ \text{Li}^{+} $ ion projected with the **same velocity** perpendicular to a magnetic field, the greatest magnetic force is felt by
items.explanation: The force is $ qvB $, and all four carry the same magnitude of charge, one elementary unit. With equal $ v $ and $ B $ the forces are identical. Mass plays no part in the *force* — only in the resulting acceleration and radius.

items.prompt: Of the same four particles projected with the same velocity perpendicular to a magnetic field, the **smallest circle** is described by
items.explanation: The radius is $ r = mv/qB $, so with equal $ v $, $ q $ and $ B $ it is proportional to mass. The electron, lighter than a proton by a factor of $ 1836 $, curls into by far the tightest circle. Same force, but far less inertia to resist it.

items.prompt: Of the same four particles, the **minimum frequency** of revolution belongs to
items.explanation: The cyclotron frequency is $ f = qB/2\pi m $, so with equal charges it is inversely proportional to mass. Lithium, the heaviest of the four, circulates most slowly. Note the frequency does not depend on the speed at all — which is precisely what makes a cyclotron workable.

items.prompt: A charged particle's velocity makes an **acute angle** with a uniform magnetic field. Its path is
items.explanation: Resolve the velocity into components along and across the field. The parallel component feels no force and stays constant; the perpendicular component circles. Together they trace a helix, and since the parallel speed never changes, the pitch is uniform.

items.prompt: A region has a uniform magnetic field and a **parallel** uniform electric field. A particle's velocity is momentarily perpendicular to both. Its path is
items.explanation: The magnetic field curls the perpendicular velocity into a circle, while the electric field — parallel to $ \vec{B} $ — steadily accelerates the particle along the axis. The circular motion continues at a fixed radius while the axial speed grows, so the helix stretches out: the pitch increases.

items.prompt: A beam containing both protons and electrons of the same speed enters a region of uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the beam. The two species
options: are deviated by different angles and separate
are deviated by the same angle and stay together
are deviated by the same angle but separate
items.explanation: Being oppositely charged they curve in *opposite* directions, and their very different masses give radii differing by a factor of $ 1836 $. So they separate decisively — which is the working principle of a mass spectrometer.

items.prompt: The work done by a magnetic force on a moving charge over any path is
options: equal to the change in kinetic energy
items.explanation: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so $ \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{s} = 0 $ at every instant. A magnetic field can bend a particle's path but never speed it up or slow it down — which is exactly why a cyclotron needs an *electric* field to do the accelerating.

sections.title: Force on Currents and Loops
sections.blurb: A current-carrying wire is a stream of moving charges.

items.prompt: A straight wire of length $ L $ carrying current $ I $ lies **parallel** to a uniform magnetic field $ B $. The force on it is
items.explanation: The force is $ BIL\sin\theta $, and with the current parallel to the field $ \theta = 0 $ so the force vanishes. It is maximum at $ BIL $ when the wire is perpendicular to the field. This is the current-carrying version of the rule that a charge moving along a field feels nothing.

items.prompt: A closed current-carrying loop of any shape is placed in a **uniform** magnetic field. The net force on it is
options: $ BIL $, where $ L $ is its perimeter
items.explanation: Summing $ Id\vec{l} \times \vec{B} $ round a closed loop involves $ \oint d\vec{l} $, which is zero because the loop returns to its start. So there is no net force — but there generally *is* a torque $ \vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B} $, and that torque is what turns an electric motor.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Force on a charge moving in a field
worked_examples.problem: A proton moves at $ 2 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ at $ 30^\circ $ to a magnetic field of $ 0.5 $ T. Find the magnetic force on it. Take $ e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} $ C.
worked_examples.solution:
$ F = qvB\sin\theta $

$ = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(2 \times 10^{6})(0.5)\sin 30^\circ $

$ = (1.6 \times 10^{-19})(2 \times 10^{6})(0.5)(0.5) $

$ = 8 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{N} $

**Direction.** Perpendicular to *both* the velocity and the field, given by the right-hand rule for $ \vec{v} \times \vec{B} $ (and reversed for a negative charge).

**Compare with gravity.** The proton's weight is $ m g \approx (1.67 \times 10^{-27})(10) = 1.7 \times 10^{-26} $ N — smaller by twelve orders of magnitude. Gravity is always ignored in charged-particle dynamics for exactly this reason.

**Note the $ \sin\theta $.** At $ 30^\circ $ only half the maximum force acts. The component of velocity *along* the field contributes nothing, which is what turns this motion into a helix rather than a circle.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Radius and period of a circular path
worked_examples.problem: An electron enters a $ 0.01 $ T field at $ 3 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $, perpendicular to the field. Find the radius of its path and the time for one revolution. Take $ m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} $ kg.
worked_examples.solution:
**Radius.** The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:

$ qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r} \Rightarrow r = \frac{mv}{qB} $

$ = \frac{(9.1 \times 10^{-31})(3 \times 10^{6})}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.01)} = \frac{2.73 \times 10^{-24}}{1.6 \times 10^{-21}} = 1.71 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} $

About $ 1.7 $ mm.

**Period:**

$ T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} = \frac{2\pi(9.1 \times 10^{-31})}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.01)} = \frac{5.72 \times 10^{-30}}{1.6 \times 10^{-21}} = 3.57 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s} $

**The remarkable feature of the period.** It contains no $ v $ — a fast electron simply traces a proportionally larger circle in the same time. This velocity-independence is what allows a cyclotron to accelerate particles with a fixed-frequency alternating voltage.

**Where it breaks down.** At relativistic speeds the mass grows, so $ T $ increases and the fixed frequency falls out of step. That is precisely why high-energy machines are *synchro*cyclotrons or synchrotrons, with a frequency that tracks the particle.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Velocity selector
worked_examples.problem: In a region, $ \vec{E} $ and $ \vec{B} $ are mutually perpendicular with $ E = 3 \times 10^{5}\ \text{V m}^{-1} $ and $ B = 0.6 $ T. Find the speed at which a charged particle passes through undeflected.
worked_examples.solution:
For no deflection, the electric and magnetic forces must cancel:

$ qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = \frac{E}{B} $

$ v = \frac{3 \times 10^{5}}{0.6} = 5 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**What makes this device useful.** The condition contains neither $ q $ nor $ m $, so it selects purely on *speed* — every particle at $ 5 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ passes straight through, whatever its charge or mass, and everything else is deflected out of the beam.

**Where it is used.** Ahead of a mass spectrometer, so that the subsequent magnetic separation reflects only $ m/q $ rather than a mixture of $ m/q $ and speed. J. J. Thomson used exactly this arrangement to measure $ e/m $ for the electron.

**A note on the geometry.** The two forces are antiparallel only for a particular orientation of $ \vec{E} $, $ \vec{B} $ and $ \vec{v} $ — all three mutually perpendicular. Reverse the particle's direction and the magnetic force flips while the electric one does not, so the balance is lost.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Cyclotron
worked_examples.problem: A cyclotron with a $ 1.5 $ T field accelerates protons to a maximum radius of $ 0.5 $ m. Find the operating frequency and the protons' maximum kinetic energy. Take $ m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} $ kg.
worked_examples.solution:
**Frequency:**

$ f = \frac{qB}{2\pi m} = \frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(1.5)}{2\pi(1.67 \times 10^{-27})} = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{1.049 \times 10^{-26}} = 2.29 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Hz} $

About $ 23 $ MHz — a radio frequency.

**Maximum speed**, at the largest radius:

$ v = \frac{qBr}{m} = \frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(1.5)(0.5)}{1.67 \times 10^{-27}} = 7.19 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Maximum kinetic energy:**

$ KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1.67 \times 10^{-27})(5.17 \times 10^{15}) = 4.3 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{J} $

In electron-volts: $ \frac{4.3 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 27\ \text{MeV} $

**How the machine works.** The magnetic field does no work at all — it merely keeps the protons circulating. All the energy comes from the alternating electric field in the gap between the dees, crossed twice per revolution.

**A caveat on the answer.** At $ 7.2 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $ the protons are moving at about $ 24\% $ of light speed, so relativistic corrections are becoming significant and the true energy is a little different. This is exactly the limit that ended the classical cyclotron's usefulness.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Force on a current-carrying wire
worked_examples.problem: A wire of length $ 20 $ cm carrying $ 5 $ A lies at $ 30^\circ $ to a $ 0.4 $ T field. Find the force on it, and the orientation for maximum force.
worked_examples.solution:
$ F = BIL\sin\theta $

$ = (0.4)(5)(0.20)\sin 30^\circ = (0.4)(5)(0.20)(0.5) = 0.2\ \text{N} $

**For maximum force**, set $ \theta = 90^\circ $ — the wire perpendicular to the field:

$ F_{max} = (0.4)(5)(0.20) = 0.4\ \text{N} $

**Where the formula comes from.** A current is $ n $ charges per unit volume drifting at $ v_d $. Summing $ qv_d B $ over all the carriers in a length $ L $ gives exactly $ BIL $ — the wire version of the single-charge force, with $ I $ absorbing $ nqv_dA $.

**Direction.** Perpendicular to both the wire and the field, from $ I\vec{L} \times \vec{B} $. Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged — which is why a d.c. motor needs a commutator to keep turning the same way.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Torque on a current loop
worked_examples.problem: A rectangular coil of $ 50 $ turns and area $ 20\ \text{cm}^{2} $ carries $ 2 $ A in a $ 0.3 $ T field, with its plane parallel to the field. Find the torque on it.
worked_examples.solution:
**Magnetic moment:**

$ M = NIA = (50)(2)(20 \times 10^{-4}) = 0.2\ \text{A m}^{2} $

**Torque:**

$ \tau = MB\sin\theta $

Here the coil's *plane* is parallel to the field, so its **normal** is perpendicular to the field and $ \theta = 90^\circ $:

$ \tau = (0.2)(0.3)(1) = 0.06\ \text{N m} $

This is the maximum possible torque for this coil.

**Watch the angle carefully.** $ \theta $ in the formula is between the field and the coil's *normal*, not its plane. 'Plane parallel to the field' therefore means $ \theta = 90^\circ $ and maximum torque — the exact opposite of what a careless reading suggests.

**Why a motor needs a commutator.** The torque falls to zero when the normal aligns with the field ($ \theta = 0 $), and beyond that point it would push the coil back. Reversing the current at that instant keeps the torque acting the same way round, which is precisely the commutator's job.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Helical path in a magnetic field
worked_examples.problem: A proton enters a $ 0.2 $ T field at $ 4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $, at $ 60^\circ $ to the field. Find the radius and pitch of its helical path.
worked_examples.solution:
**Resolve the velocity.**

Perpendicular to $ \vec{B} $: $ v_\perp = v\sin 60^\circ = (4 \times 10^{5})(0.866) = 3.46 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

Parallel to $ \vec{B} $: $ v_\parallel = v\cos 60^\circ = 2 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Radius**, set by the perpendicular component only:

$ r = \frac{mv_\perp}{qB} = \frac{(1.67 \times 10^{-27})(3.46 \times 10^{5})}{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(0.2)} = \frac{5.78 \times 10^{-22}}{3.2 \times 10^{-20}} = 0.0181\ \text{m} $

**Period:**

$ T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} = \frac{2\pi(1.67 \times 10^{-27})}{3.2 \times 10^{-20}} = 3.28 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{s} $

**Pitch** — the axial advance in one revolution:

$ p = v_\parallel T = (2 \times 10^{5})(3.28 \times 10^{-7}) = 0.066\ \text{m} $

**The division of labour.** The perpendicular component sets the radius; the parallel component sets the pitch; and the period depends on neither. That separation is what makes helical motion tractable — treat the two components independently and recombine at the end.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Mass spectrometer
worked_examples.problem: Singly charged ions of neon-20 and neon-22 are accelerated through $ 1000 $ V and then enter a $ 0.5 $ T field perpendicular to their motion. Find the ratio of their path radii. Take $ 1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} $ kg.
worked_examples.solution:
**Speed after acceleration** through a potential difference $ V $:

$ qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}} $

**Radius in the field:**

$ r = \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{m}{qB}\sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}} = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}} $

So $ r \propto \sqrt{m} $ for equal charge and accelerating voltage.

**Ratio:**

$ \frac{r_{22}}{r_{20}} = \sqrt{\frac{22}{20}} = \sqrt{1.1} = 1.049 $

The heavier isotope's radius is about $ 4.9\% $ larger.

**Why that small difference is enough.** With radii of, say, $ 20 $ cm, a $ 4.9\% $ gap is nearly a centimetre at the detector — easily resolved. Mass spectrometry can separate isotopes differing by a single neutron precisely because the geometry amplifies the difference.

**Note the square root.** Radius goes as $ \sqrt{m} $, not $ m $, because the heavier ion also emerges from the accelerator more slowly. Two competing effects, and the square root is what survives.
